demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.explanation: For trauma type 'unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one', the body-focused appraisals 'I can no longer trust my own body' and 'I feel ashamed of what happened to my body' are hard to reconcile clinically unless the patient also directly experienced major bodily violation/injury, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

The memory items imply vivid sensory reliving of the traumatic event ('hear things ... heard during the frightening event') and fragmented visual snapshots, which can occur in PTSD, but here they are not well matched to the selected appraisals: the profile centers on bodily shame/unreliability rather than grief/death-related meanings of the event.

'Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study' is not impossible, but in this profile it appears weakly integrated: there are no trigger or threat items tying work contexts to the trauma, and the formulation does not include trigger/threat pathways. The coping profile otherwise concerns sleep delay and undereating, so work avoidance feels insufficiently anchored.

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one, body-focused shame is clinically hard to reconcile unless there was also direct bodily violation, injury, or assault. The rest of the profile centers grief-related loss, meaning, and intrusive memory phenomena, so this item appears inconsistent with the trauma type and with the other selected items.

vignette:
Mere Tuilagi is a 46-year-old Fijian-American woman who works as a forensic analyst for a county crime laboratory. She is married and lives with her husband in a mid-sized city in the Pacific Northwest. She was referred for psychological assessment following a PCL-5 score of 78, obtained after her primary care physician became concerned about her deteriorating physical health and what she described, in her own words, as "not being able to function anymore."

Eleven months ago, Mere received a phone call at her workstation - surrounded by evidence bags and case files - informing her that her younger sister, Lani, had been killed in a road accident. The call came on an ordinary Tuesday afternoon. Mere later described the sound of the dispatcher's voice as something she could not unhear: a flat, procedural tone delivering words that seemed to arrive from outside of time. She drove to the hospital alone. What she found there - the clinical whiteness of the corridor, the sound of a monitor still alarmed in a room she was not allowed to enter, the particular silence that followed - became the material from which her memory of the event is now constructed. She does not recall it as a continuous narrative. Instead, it exists in her mind as a series of fixed images: the fluorescent light above the reception desk, the grain of the linoleum floor where she stood when a nurse told her Lani was gone, the shape of her own hands in her lap in the car afterward. Each image is vivid and complete, like a photograph, and each carries with it the sound that accompanied it - the alarm, the nurse's voice, the silence. When the memory returns, it does so without warning, and Mere has described being so overwhelmed by the emotion it carries that she has to stop whatever she is doing entirely, sometimes sitting motionless at her desk for minutes at a time before she can recover herself.

In the months that followed, Mere came to believe, with a conviction she found difficult to articulate but impossible to dismiss, that her life had been fundamentally and irreversibly destroyed. She had lost her faith - in the predictability of the world, in the fairness she had once assumed operated beneath ordinary events, in the religious practice that had anchored her Fijian upbringing. Nothing she did felt like it carried weight or purpose. These appraisals - that meaning was gone, that people and life itself could not be trusted - began to shape her behaviour in ways that felt, to Mere, entirely logical. If nothing mattered, there was no reason to face the day. She began calling in sick to the forensic laboratory with increasing frequency, and on the days she did go in, she found herself unable to process case materials without the images returning - the evidence photographs, the chain-of-custody documents, the clinical language of harm - all of it resonating with the visual and auditory texture of the hospital corridor. Her supervisor has noted a significant decline in her output, and two cases have been reassigned. Mere is aware of this. She experiences it as confirmation rather than consequence.

At home, she began staying up until two or three in the morning, not from insomnia precisely but from a deliberate reluctance to enter the vulnerability of sleep, where she had less control over what returned to her. She also began eating very little - skipping meals, reducing portions - not from appetite loss alone but as a form of management, a way of imposing some structure on a body that otherwise felt ungoverned. These strategies, however, did not contain the memories. The sleep deprivation and the physical depletion that followed the restricted eating left her cognitively and emotionally raw, so that when the auditory and visual fragments of the hospital did surface, she had fewer resources to absorb them, and the overwhelm was more complete. The exhaustion, in turn, reinforced her certainty that she was broken - that someone who could not sleep, could not eat, could not go to work was someone whose life had, in fact, been destroyed - and this belief made it harder still to imagine that returning to the laboratory or sitting at the dinner table could mean anything at all.

What finally brought Mere to seek help was her husband, who told her quietly one evening that he was frightened he was losing her. She did not disagree with him. What she is most afraid of is that he is right. What she is most hoping for, though she struggles to say it plainly, is that something in her can still be reached.
